subjects.label: Nobility: loss of privilege and social transformation
subjects.meaning: The Revolution ended noble corporate status, feudal and fiscal privilege, venal ennoblement and automatic deference. Emigration, confiscation, execution and failed return caused trauma, but property recovery and later elite continuity limit any claim of total material destruction.
subjects.stance: Many nobles had supported reform before polemic cast aristocracy as a universal enemy. Nobles lost public monopoly and presumed social subordination more decisively than wealth; ending purchased ennoblement paradoxically made surviving social nobility more caste-like.

evidence.evidence_summary: Anti-noble rhetoric and conflict over separate representation turned a reform-minded order into presumed enemies of regeneration.
Political, fiscal, feudal, and heraldic privileges disappeared, altering nobility from an open elite into an inherited caste.
Exile, Quiberon, suspicion and diminished public influence deepened hostility; psychological displacement and loss of automatic deference were more enduring than the nobles’ material losses.
